overview: Kerma was the capital of a Nubian kingdom on the Nile in present-day Sudan. Its prosperity rested on herding, cultivation and exchange between African interiors and Egypt. This page follows the kingdom, its earlier background and what archaeology reveals about its people.

periods.title: Before the kingdom: Pre-Kerma
periods.summary: This is the earlier Pre-Kerma settlement phase, not the later kingdom. Excavations reveal huts, cattle enclosures and storage pits; its political organization and territorial extent remain uncertain.

periods.title: Early Kerma
periods.summary: The royal city and its cemetery develop. Archaeological dates for this beginning are approximate, around 2500 to 2450 BCE.

periods.title: Middle Kerma
periods.summary: Fortified walls, a palace and increasingly elaborate burials reveal a more strongly differentiated society.

periods.title: Classical Kerma
periods.summary: Major temple building, urban expansion and monumental royal graves mark the kingdom's most imposing phase. These archaeological phase boundaries are approximate.

periods.title: Conquest and transition
periods.summary: The mission identifies a Final Kerma transition as Egyptian rule takes hold. Conquest unfolded through campaigns and local resistance, not one securely dated event.

items.text: Excavators mapped houses with courtyards containing kitchens and grain silos. These remains show how households organized cooking and storage around shared outdoor space.

Temple workshops and storerooms clustered around the Western Deffufa. A palace contained a large circular building interpreted as a royal audience hall, revealing distinct religious and political spaces.
At Middle Kerma grave 253, researchers recorded 4,899 cattle skulls. They interpret the association between large tombs and numerous skulls as a display of the deceased person's wealth and power.

Some cattle horns had been deliberately reshaped; cut marks and altered growth preserve evidence of the practice. Researchers suggest specially valued animals were distinguished this way, while warning against copying modern herders' beliefs directly onto ancient Kerma.

Kerma potters shaped exceptionally thin cups by hand, then polished their red surfaces. Controlled firing produced black rims and interiors, evidence of skilled handling of both clay and the firing atmosphere.
A tulip-shaped beaker in Manchester Museum was excavated at Kerma in 1913. Its smooth, shining finish was made by burnishing the clay before firing; the form was achieved without a potter's wheel.
Cattle also appeared in small figurines found in the city and in paintings in a funerary chapel. Their presence in art as well as graves suggests a significance extending beyond food and exchange.

Animal bones from the capital show that domestic livestock supplied most of the meat evidence. Cattle, sheep and goats dominated; the researchers observed a later increase in sheep and goats relative to cattle.

Fine beakers existed alongside heavier storage jars, sometimes stamped around the rim. Stone implements remained in use beside metal technology, preserving evidence of practical choices in everyday tools.

Graves preserve wooden beds, personal ornaments, sandals and containers for oils or ointments. Larger, richer tombs show growing inequality; some also contained accompanying people interpreted as victims of funerary killing.

A Kerma-style beaker now at the Metropolitan Museum was excavated at Abydos in Egypt. Such finds demonstrate connections across the Nile Valley, but the museum cautions that pottery alone cannot establish whether the people buried with it were Nubian traders.

Survey finds include Egyptian pottery together with Nubian pottery. Stuart Tyson Smith interprets the settlement pattern as evidence that some local elites retained cultural and political latitude under Egyptian rule; conquest did not erase Nubian society.

The relationship between the earlier Pre-Kerma settlement and the royal city is not fully demonstrated. Excavated buildings and objects reveal much, but their locations do not establish precise kingdom borders.

ending.text: Egyptian New Kingdom campaigns ended Kerma's independence. The excavation mission places the capital's destruction around 1450 BCE, after a longer conquest associated with Thutmose I and Thutmose III; this is an approximate endpoint, not a known single day of collapse.
